maintopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER OF GREECE AND PARTY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER OF GREECE AND PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have today in the gallery a representative, the Prime Minister, of an ally of Canada's-Prime Minister Karamanlis of Greece. He will already, by the reception accorded to him by the members, realize the warmth of our feelings toward his country. He is accompanied by his wife as well as by the foreign minister of Greece, Mr. Averoff-Tossizza.
Yesterday we had the opportunity of discussing together matters of interest not only to our two countries but, as well, to the strengthening of the bonds of NATO and the assurance that Canada in the days ahead will be able to meet its responsibilities as it has since the date of the formation of NATO. In this connection it is well for the house to note that he has joined with the viewpoint of Canada in believing that it is most necessary, at the earliest date convenient, considering the preparation that must be made in order to achieve the greatest success, to have a meeting of the heads of state among NATO leaders. It is a necessity, having regard to the situation in NATO and in the international field as well.
We welcome him for himself and for the contribution he has made to the stability of his own country. We welcome him as the representative of a member nation in that organization of which I have just spoken. We welcome him for the contribution to and the heritage of culture that his country has given not only to the western civilization but to democracy and its principles throughout the world. We welcome him as the leader of a nation which has given much to Canada in the thousands of immigrants from that country who have come to us and joined in the building of Canadianism, and in the contribution which, in every part of Canada, is made by people of his race.
Therefore, sir, I draw your attention to the fact that he is here, and I again welcome to this country a true friend, an outstanding statesman, one whose dedication and whose
country's dedication to freedom and democracy makes stronger the NATO organization and freedom itself everywhere in the world.

maintopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER OF GREECE AND PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition, whose absence I greatly regret-an absence that is quite unavoidable-I should like on behalf of our friends to join with the Prime Minister, whose every word I echo, in welcoming the Prime Minister of Greece and those who are with him as visitors to this country today. While I regret the absence of the Leader of the Opposition, it is perhaps not unfitting that a representative of the greatest sea-faring people in the new world should welcome this representative of the first great sea-faring nation of the old world.
If I may be even more personal and recall my youth in the bush in northern Manitoba, one of the most distinguished of the citizens of that community was an immigrant from Greece, whose family were honoured in that community then and are honoured still today. All of us remember from our school days the warning timeo Danaos et dona ferentes, but no one who sits in a free parliament fears the greatest of all the gifts of the Greeks to the world, the idea of selfgovernment, and for that we are eternally grateful to the people represented by the prime minister who is our guest today. Nor shall we forget, sir, that it was the language of Greece which was the vehicle for the spread of the religion most of us profess in Canada. We remember too how Greece fought and suffered for freedom in the dark days of the war. We remember that from the days of Byron to the days of Harry Truman, modern Greece has been on the frontiers of freedom. We are happy that Greece, which has perhaps historically the greatest claim to be the champion of freedom, as the Prime Minister has reminded us, is an integral member of that society of free nations, the North Atlantic alliance, which all of us, I trust, want to see strengthened in every way possible in order to meet the difficulties with which we are faced in the free world of today.

maintopic: WELCOME TO PRIME MINISTER OF GREECE AND PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in adding our words of welcome to Canada to the

Inquiries of the Ministry Prime Minister of Greece. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who is very often at sea, was probably more appropriately at sea this morning in many of the remarks he made.
We acknowledge that the Prime Minister of Greece, our guest today, was himself instrumental in bringing about peace and independence to the island of Cyprus. The Prime Minister has associated the Prime Minister of Greece with his own views on certain aspects of the NATO organization. We do not agree with all of his comments in that particular regard, but realizing that Greece has done so much for the development and independence of free institutions of the world, we do welcome her prime minister.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked a question concerning export financing. In reply I wish to state that following my announcement in the house last November 25 on export financing, two new institutions have been established for this purpose. They are the Export Finance Corporation of Canada Limited, a private institution wholly owned by the nine chartered banks, and the export finance division of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, which is a government agency.
The Export Finance Corporation, using private funds, will finance exports for periods up to five years. The charter of this corporation provides for a subscribed capital of $50 million, with the right to borrow 10 times this amount, for example, up to $500 million, to finance exports from Canada. I understand that to date only $10 million of the subscribed capital has been paid in and the Export Finance Corporation is therefore in a position to borrow and undertake financing up to an
[Mr. Argue.l
amount of $100 million. This amount will of course increase as larger percentages of the subscribed capital are paid in.
The Export Finance Corporation has only recently commenced operations and I am not in a position to give information on the amount of export financing which it may have undertaken. It is my understanding, however, that it has not undertaken any substantial amount of export financing as yet. I would like to emphasize that the Export Finance Corporation is a private corporation which will undertake financing for periods not in excess of five years and that no public funds are involved in its export financing operations.
The export finance division of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation is the government institution which will handle the government's export financing program. Two hundred million dollars is the sum available for this program under the present provisions of sections 21 and 21A of the Export Credits Insurance Act. In so far as the government is concerned, the basic principle of its export financing program is that the government is now in a position to finance the export of capital goods for periods ranging from five to fifteen years, or longer, at rates of interest approximately equal to those being offered by major competitors. Government financing is, however, available only for capital goods having a high Canadian content (eighty per cent) minimum and which are intended for use in economically sound projects in creditworthy countries wherein it is reasonable to expect continuing foreign sales.
Although the export finance division has been in operation only for the past three months, Canadian exporters have already applied for extended term financing for 18 projects for transactions in 11 countries, to a total value of approximately $213 million. All such applications are considered by an interdepartmental committee known as the committee on export finance, which determines, in the light of the principles and procedures regulating government export financing, whether applications should be submitted to cabinet for approval. Of the $213 million of applications thus far received, $52| million have already been judged suitable for submission to cabinet and the remainder are receiving careful examination. I would like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian exporters are in a position to bid for this potential new business amounting to $213 million solely by reason of the establishment of the government's long term lending program.
In conclusion, I would like to state that although there is no direct relationship

between the government's winter works program and the long term export financing program, it is a fact that economic and employment considerations within Canada are an important criterion for determining whether or not an application for export financing should be granted.

Last night, Mr. Chairman, my theme was the perfect Postmaster General that we have in Canada at the present time.
Oh, oh.

I wonder why the Prime Minister should want to hire John Fisher away from touting Anaconda Brass or Niagara Finance when he has this advertising genius in the ranks of the cabinet. We know from the last paragraph of his speech yesterday that his department has moved into a state of perfection, within no limits. It seems to me we now have a minister who is at a level from which he can move on to greater and greater responsibilities, perhaps to a more important department.
For that reason I should like to draw to the attention of all hon. members of the committee a speech made by the Postmaster General, to which I referred last night and which was reprinted in a publication entitled "Vital Speeches of Today", dated March 1, 1961, in which the minister makes a statement on

United States-Canadian relations and sets out Canadian government policy in this very important field.
I say again that I am afraid he is such a perfect Postmaster General we may not have him much longer as such. He will be moved to greater and more expansive realms. If he should move into a field in which he could devote his tendency to the hard sell, rather than the soft sell, I would imagine he would be selling the doctrine of free enterprise and the new frontier that has been announced by the Prime Minister.
This is interesting to me, because the Post Office Department has quite an odd interest in free enterprise and in supporting free enterprise. One of the things the Postmaster General indicated last year, apparently as a result of some questions I asked him, was that every three or four years the Post Office Department makes an analysis of its operations from the point of view of costs. We have an indication in the speech he gave yesterday that the increase in parcel post rates is the result of one of these investigations. This investigation revealed there was a deficit in connection with the operation, so the rates were increased.
Last year the Postmaster General indicated in information he gave me in reply to question No. 34 on the order paper, which concerned the estimates of loss or profit on second class mail, that during the fiscal year 1958-59, based on the department's calculations, the estimated excess of disbursements over receipts amounted to $21,690,000 for newspapers and periodicals. The revenue in that particular year was only $6,189,125. In other words there was a disparity of some $15 million. We have had no indication in the annual report or in the minister's speech as to whether or not this loss has continued. We know that certain subjects have been considered by the royal commission on publications in this connection.
I must come back to this theme of free enterprise and the part the Postmaster General and his department are playing in supporting free enterprise in this country. I wonder how many members of the house have ever heard of the Siftons, the McConnells, the Thomsons or the Welds, and have ever considered that they were poor people. Are the McConnells, the Siftons, the Thomsons and the Welds in this country poor people? I think the answer is of course a ringing "No". No one needs to be told of the tremendous fortune, at least in terms of assets, that Roy Thomson has built up so that now he is a colossus bestriding the whole publishing field, not only in Canada but in Great Britain. Yet the minister and his department
Supply-Post Office
have helped to subsidize these free enterprises of the Thomsons, the McConnells, the Siftons and the Welds.
I give one example in connection with the second class mailing rates. The postage rate, supposedly, in Canada has been kept low on second class publications because they wanted low subscription rates for the farmers. The three biggest publishers of farm periodicals in Canada are the McConnell interests of Montreal, with the Family Herald and Weekly Star; the Sifton interests of Winnipeg, with the Free Press Prairie Farmer, and the Weld family of London, Ontario, with the Farmer's Advocate. I would say that the McConnells and the Siftons probably rank among the wealthiest families and interests in Canada. A great deal of their wealth has come from their publishing empires and from these fantastically successful and very able publications, the Family Herald and Weekly Star and the Free Press Prairie Farmer.
In the light of this kind of wealth I wonder how much longer we have to go on subsidizing not only the farmer, who benefits by cheaper subscriptions, but these wealthy men. It seems to me that we need a real analysis carried out here. If I had any idea that the McConnells, the Siftons or the Welds were about to go to the wall and were near a state of bankruptcy; if I thought Roy Thomson was in a state of collapse financially, I could see why we should continue to give these low postal rates. But this is not true as far as I know. We have had no indication that these big empires of commerce are shaky. As a matter of fact they seem to be getting bigger and better.
Yet their main publications, and certainly I think the publications that probably bring them in the most income, are among the ones that are piling up this terrific deficit for the Post Office Department. I think the minister will acknowledge that there is in Canada a special rate for daily newspapers having a circulation of less than 10,000 a day. What publisher in Canada owns the most daily newspapers with a circulation of less than 10,000 a day? Some poor, struggling fellow who is trying to get along? Are there many of them who are still trying to keep their heads above water? No; it is our friend Roy Thomson.
The Kamloops Sentinel has an estimated circulation, according to the latest figures, of approximately 6,500; the Kelowna Courier 5,100; the Nanaimo Free Press 8,100; the Penticton Herald 4,800:	the Moose Jaw
Times-Herald 7,900; the Prince Albert Herald 6,800; the Barrie Examiner 8,100; the Kirkland Lake Northern News 6,200; the Orillia Packet and Times 5,700:	the

Supply-Post Office
Pembroke Observer 6,600; the Woodstock Sentinel Review 9,600 and the Quebec city Chronicle-Telegraph 5,600. These are all newspapers with a circulation of less than 10,000 a day; they are owned by Roy Thomson of the Thomson interests, and they all have a special rate. To me this is one of the most insidious forms of subsidy. It is the kind of subsidy that goes to a free enterpriser who is always shoving free enterprise down our craw.
We have a Thomson paper in our area. Recently it has shown some marked improvement in certain ways in my opinion. I follow the Thomson newspapers fairly closely, and one of their favourite lines is attacking the C.B.C. and the Canada council by advocating the throwing out of such subsidies and saying these agencies are wasting the taxpayers' money. We have a deficit of $20 million in one branch of the Post Office Department- it is not quite a deficit; it is an estimated deficit-and among the prime beneficiaries in Canada is the Thomson chain.
I would have some sympathy for the Thomson papers if they were carrying the odd story or writing the odd editorial on the fact that the Post Office Department is losing money on second class mail. But you do not get that. Instead you get this constant war of attrition against the C.B.C., the Canada council and the C.N.R., these profligate wasters of the taxpayers' money.
This is the kind of insidious inconsistency in the free enterprise approach upon which I should like to hear the minister speak. Are we still subsidizing the poor farmer in bringing him this wonderful information which he obtains from the daily newspapers or the farming publications, or are we subsidizing the McConnells, the Siftons and the Thomsons? I would like an answer to that question.
While I admire the self-made man who can go ahead and build himself a fortune and an empire, not only here but in the world itself, I think we should look at the situation very closely if part of that wealth is accruing in an indirect way by means of subsidy from the Canadian taxpayer. I think it is only fair, in terms of the critique that these gentlemen and their newspapers themselves apply. For that reason I think we should know more about the estimates of the Postmaster General and the costs of delivering this periodical mail.
I know this matter is confused by a fact which is, in a way, a much more important issue. I refer to the fact that at the present time we are not only subsidizing the McConnells, the Siftons, the Welds and the Thomsons, but Time magazine, Reader's Digest and

all the other United States publications that come into this country at a fantastically low rate, considering weight and distance carried, in comparison with Canadian publications.
As I say, the one problem tends to dwarf the other, but no person can look at the information given to me and realize the importance of this matter. I would like to put this information on the record, but the Postmaster General remarked his letter "personal and confidential". This was a letter he sent me on July 27, 1960. It was a four page letter which I appreciated; it was full of information on this very point.
However, the Post Office Department is losing money on carrying second class mail. The Postmaster General has the figures here to substantiate this statement. They are especially losing money on carrying United States' periodicals. As I remember from the figures given to the royal commission, the 45 leading United States magazines have a circulation in Canada of over 61 million, while the eight Canadian magazines that are in comparable fields have a circulation of a little over two million. Therefore there is no question about it, the United States publications have a great advantage over comparable Canadian publications since they are generally heavier and carried further.
However, I still insist that as much as we hope this will be corrected by the royal commission, this is no excuse at all for any longer giving subsidies to men of such substance who control the farming publications and these daily newspapers with a circulation of less than 10,000.
The argument can probably be made, do you want to put the poor people in Prince Albert in the situation where they can only get news about the Prime Minister at a higher price, because this would mean higher priced newspapers? All I can say is that we do not know what profits Mr. Thomson has made from the Prince Albert paper or any of these other papers. It is none of our business. But we assume that he has done very well, because he started with a small radio station in Kirkland Lake, moved to a few newspapers and now has a chain across Canada, some in the United States, he is going down into Africa and he almost sewed up the periodical market in the United Kingdom.
I do not believe money is created magically, or the resources for this kind of empire. It came from somewhere. Where did that money come from? I think we have to assume that it came from the little people in Prince Albert, Kelowna, Woodstock, and so on. If this is the case, I think we deserve a check on the particular aspect I have raised. How much

longer are these special rates on agricultural publications and publications with circulation of less than 10,000 or less to be carried on?
I did want to make some complimentary remarks about the employees of the department as well as about the minister. The thing I like about post office employees, and I can say this because I would not say it about very many civil servants, is that they have a lot of militancy and fibre. They have great solidarity. I was delighted to read in this morning's paper that the representative appearing before a house committee took a very strong line on collective bargaining. I enjoy reading the Postal Journal of Canada. It is about the most forthright of all the publications put out by the civil service associations. I must pay the minister at least an indirect compliment by saying I have seen no falling away since he took office in either the militancy or the self reliance or the fibre of the employees. More power to them, and I wish more civil servants had the same attitude as the majority of postal employees.
There is one other aspect of the general question on which I should like to hear the minister's comments. A publication appeared recently which contains a great deal of information on public administration in Canada. It is really an editors' job by Hodgetts and Corbett called "Canadian Public Administration". Included in it is a very fine article by a former senior civil servant of the department, Mr. Turnbull, entitled "Decentralization in the Post Office". This essay was first published approximately six years ago and it indicates that decentralization was already taking place in the department with a promise that it would bring better controls, reduced costs, and so on.
The question I should like to ask the minister in the light, I was about to say, of the bragging-or perhaps I had better call it the complimentary way he has looked at the operations of the post office since they came within his grasp-is whether some of these advances have come about as a result of this policy of decentralization which followed the Woods Gordon report of six or seven years ago, and about which Mr. Turnbull has written. I mention this because I think the minister may in all modesty want to give some credit, if not to his ministerial predecessor then at least to some of the senior civil servants under the former government who might have set up changes the benefits of which are now being reaped so brilliantly, or so forcefully, or in such a hard sell manner by the present Postmaster General.
There is one other point with which I should like to deal. It is a more specific point, and one on which I should like to have some information from the Postmaster General. I
Supply-Post Office
should like to know what steps he has taken to stop the development of football sweeps and lotteries of all kinds in Canada. I have brought this matter up before. The two Toronto evening papers, the Toronto Telegram and the Toronto Star, carry, every Wednesday I think it is, the results of a certain football pool in England. I am no legal expert, but it seems to me those pool results indicate- and this I know because some of my friends are involved-that a good many people are playing the football pools in England, and they may or may not be using the mails. I am fairly certain they are, and I think I know how they are getting round the provisions against doing so. The point is that neither the Toronto Telegram nor the Toronto Star would be carrying these excerpts of information if they did not know that there was an interest, and a substantial interest in what is, according to the minister's own actions, an illegal enterprise in Canada. I should like to know from the minister, since his officials have gone to the trouble of opening the mail of some of those little people who are playing the football pools in England, whether he is considering doing anything about stopping the passage by mail of those newspapers which are carrying football pool information.
I refuse to believe that this information, carried regularly every Wednesday evening, giving the winnings and the ratios for the various parts of the pool, is given because Canadians have an altruistic interest in it. I suggest the information is carried because it is known that Canadians are playing these football pools. I believe we should be allowed to play them. That is my personal stand, not a party position at all. If the minister is going to be consistent, what is he going to do about this publication in newspapers, which go through the mails, of information on illegal activities?
I cannot myself make out whether this information is inserted as news or as an advertisement. I have written to one of the newspapers on the point and received no reply. I asked the correspondent of another newspaper to check, and he told me he had received no reply. We do not know whether this information is an advertisement or news. However, I suggest that the regularity with which this information is inserted is something the minister should investigate if he is going to run around opening the mail of the little people who play the pools.

Would the hon. member permit a question? The hon. member indicated that he was giving his personal expression of opinion concerning these football pools and not an expression of party opinion. If we had a Canadian lottery in Canada I think the problem would be obviated, and

Supply-Post Office
I was wondering whether the hon. member could speak for his party and indicate whether they are in favour of a lottery in Canada.

speechtext: I would have some objection to the nature of the debate being changed.

On the point of order, the hon. member has been complaining about the fact that information useful to people who are playing football pools is passing through the mails. I was suggesting that if we had a Canadian lottery the difficulty would be obviated, because those who are now playing the Old Country football pools would then be in a position to play them in Canada. I was trying to find out, since the hon. member has given his personal opinion, whether or not his party is in favour of a Canadian lottery.
I can only refer hon. members to what X think was an excellent speech I made about a month after the house-
Oh.
Well, this is not a time for modesty. If I am going to play in the Postmaster General's league I have to adopt some of his tactics.
You do not know where your party stands.

It includes a most peculiar little statement, which I will read:
Should this be contrary to your beliefs kindly accept our apology and disregard this advertising. Please feel assured it is unlikely that you will hear from us again.

If you look at newspapers, such as the Family Herald and Weekly Star, you will find in the classified section all kinds of this type of advertising. What will happen if this type of thing leads to a massive assault upon Canadian householders? What can the Postmaster General do to protect people from receiving this kind of information which stresses that these things are designed solely with regard to health but happen to have, I think it is commonly agreed, a more practical objective?
I suggest that this is something that should be investigated. I certainly object generally to the amount of direct mail that householders receive. I know as politicians and members of parliament we probably receive more direct mail than any other group of people in Canada, which is perhaps as it should be, but why the ordinary householder should be bombarded in this way is something I do not understand, especially in regard to subjects as personal as this. It seems to me that the post office should consider whether the circulation of this kind of information falls within some part of the Criminal Code which makes it illegal. If an individual writes for this kind of information in following up an advertisement appearing in the newspapers that is quite all right, but to receive this kind of information out of a clear blue sky is something of a different nature.
This particular advertisement came from Twin Cities Sales of Winnipeg but, considering the many companies in Canada in this field, if they all follow this type of advertising, using

mailing lists or telephone directories, the post office will be faced with a very serious problem. I would like to know what the minister feels his officials can do in this regard, or what advice they can supply those people who receive this kind of information. In this regard, a well deserved tribute must be paid the present Postmaster General for having done his duty according to his conscience. Is it not a fact that the first postmaster or the first postal employee to be dismissed after the election of the Conservative party was so dismissed as the result of a complaint or recommendation from a Liberal member?
That is how the minister goes about discharging his duties. Therefore, instead of showering abuse upon him, and directing all kinds of innuendoes, as the hon. member for St. Denis did yesterday, we should be taking our hats off to the minister and telling him that he is fulfilling his duties to the satisfaction of all.
I wish the person who was in the gallery yesterday and was so amused by the act of buffoonery being put on by the hon. member for St. Denis, were here today and gave other members the same publicity he gave to the clowning of our friend from St. Denis. But this man is here only when it suits him. I therefore appeal to his colleague who I feel [Mr. Ricard.}
is more imbued with a sense of duty towards his obligations and is more capable of following the dictates of his conscience rather than being beholden to a party.

A good Postmaster General must at the same time be a good administrator. He should be able to honour his pledges, and also display great humanity in his relations with his staff. The Postmaster General, a good administrator? I want to be fair with him. I only ask him to prove it. He has been Postmaster General for four years now and he has not yet done so. A man who is true to his promises? I have before me four or five clear cases of promises he made while he was sitting on this side of the house. If he does not yet know it, we are now going through the worst unemployment crisis ever experienced since the Conservative or Tory depression of the thirties. We remember that, when the minister was sitting on this side of the house-the official record is there to show it l16 it was preposterous to maintain that post office savings bank because, he used to say, it was unnecessary competing with the chartered banks. "The banks are able to provide all necessary services to the public; that post office savings bank is therefore useless , he used to say. Well today the banks have increased their services to the public. Therefore, if this was true between 1953 and 1957, it is even more so today. Today, we can drive over to a bank even at night

and make a deposit. Mr. Chairman, between 1953 and 1957, the minister was often heard on the subject of twice daily deliveries of mail in urban areas.
He has now been heading this department for four years and nothing has been done. That is another unkept promise, one gone with the wind.

Therefore to code all the letters is a useless task, especially if, as anticipated, they could be processed by a machine which would automatically face them up. I could also make other comments about his remarks on mechanization and automation, as well as about the remarks made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets), who asked that mechanization be discarded and that some devices used in post offices be removed in order to guarantee employment.
Well, if that were put into practice, I think we would go back to the horse and buggy era, or to the full use of labour.

There is only one small thing I would like to suggest to the minister. First I would acknowledge that, contrary to what has been said about the morale of postal officers throughout the country, in my particular region I enjoy a very favourable relationship with them. I have received the utmost courtesy from them, and certainly none have complained to me as to their positions. As a matter of fact the situation is rather to the contrary. I have had very laudatory letters about the administration and consideration that this government has given to the postal employees.
The one point I would like to bring to the minister's attention is to suggest that in the regulations which are now interpreted as being in force in respect of direct carrier service to new subdivisions, perhaps a different principle should be applied. Some years ago when I moved to a new subdivision, and I was one of the first there, I had to wait ten or 11 months for postal service, and was highly incensed about what I felt was a rather high and mighty attitude in respect of postal delivery service taken by the department. It seemed to me that the service was provided the citizens of this country through the beneficence of some benevolent power and one had to petition and finally, if all things were done according to the regulations, perhaps postal service would be furnished. When I indicated that I

felt that the Post Office Department might be interested in our affairs in the same way the milkman, the newspaper boy, the baker and magazine salesmen were, who after all do not run a greater risk of falling down a drainage ditch or a sunken excavation for a sewage system, these excuses of regulations were given to me as to why services could not be provided until a red carpet was practically rolled out for the postman.
May I say in all fairness that I think there has been some adjustment in this regard, and that the regulations are not now so stringent. I would point out, however, that when people move out to new subdivisions they move there permanently and are not likely to try to escape or run away; and if the milkman, dry cleaner, baker and newspaper boy find it possible and convenient to get around, not only by machine but on foot, in areas where streets and fully completed sidewalks do not exist-after all these subdivisions are not built exactly in swamps or quagmires-perhaps mail service could be provided a little sooner than has been the case. I know there are the group box systems which do provide welcome relief from the full application of the restrictions, but I suggest to the Postmaster General that this matter could perhaps be reviewed so that somewhat more rapid service could be provided in the urban subdivisions. I am particularly interested in this problem because the area in which I live is one of the fastest growing urban areas in the country, and I have received many complaints and met with many difficulties in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the minister's speech and I noted with what pride he dealt with the achievements of and the developments in his department. As a matter of fact, while he was speaking I could not help but have several Shakespearean couplets run through my mind. I cannot take time to deal with those which came to mind except to say he did remind me of Henry V addressing the troops before the battle of Agincourt; and I paraphrase: "Here we come; here we fight; here we stay to fight again another day".
However, Mr. Chairman, I think it is a truism to say that the minister is a minister
Supply-Post Office
of socialist enterprises. I was glad to note how proud he was to be the minister of such a department, one of the most successful departments of the government because there is so little controversy as to policy. If only that principle could be applied, say, to the department of the Minister of Public Works, what progress we would make in this house.
When the minister was speaking I expected for a moment or two to see another halo descend around another member of the cabinet. I have seen a picture of one around the Prime Minister and I thought possibly the Postmaster General was likely to have one descend on him. However, while he was speaking the door of memory was held ajar. What a contrast between the minister of today and, shall I say, the ordinary member of almost yesterday who held up the estimates of the Postmaster General for two days almost single handed. We sat close to one another. I heard his every word and witnessed his every action, two days of caustic criticism of the Post Office Department for failing to have twice-a-day mail delivery. I do not think we yet have twice-a-day mail delivery across Canada. His captious condemnation of departmental administration and what I thought at that time was his callow, ceaseless carping on the details of the departmental administration, about which he apparently knew very little, come to mind.
However, we now have a symbol of democratic evolution. We have a demonstration once again, so often found in British history, that with the descent of the mantle of office come responsibility, understanding and appreciation.
Before going on with my further remarks, I must say that I appreciate the minister's prompt and courteous attention to any matter or complaint that I have brought to his notice. I cannot help but remember, though, that on one occasion he was a bit snappy with me. Later, when he found out I was right, he came and told me so; he wrote me and told me that I was right and I appreciate it. I tell him quite sincerely that all is forgiven.
Thank you; I have so much humility.

I must also express my appreciation of the work of the Ottawa district staffs throughout the country and even of the humblest employee. When we are discussing estimates like these we must remember that this department functions only as a result of co-operation between the top and the bottom, and even the humblest employee carrying the mail and doing these

other tasks, which are necessary to perform this great service, is from the democratic socialist point of view-I do not know whether it would be from the point of view of the Minister of Public Works-performing, as the minister is in his position, an equal and necessary service for the state.

I do suggest, as I think any fair person who has had any association with the Post Office Department realizes, that in recent years there has been a great improvement in morale. There was a period at one time when I and others considered that the morale of the postal employees was pretty low but there has been a general improvement owing to improvements in administration and working conditions and also improvement in the relations between the officials at the top and the humblest employee at the bottom, which means a great deal. I hope the minister will give every consideration to the needs and proper requests of a devoted and loyal staff throughout the country with respect to salary increases, working conditions, pensions, seniority and things of that sort.
I want to say a word or two about the annual report of the minister's department. First of all, let me say that I think it is most attractive. It is well organized as far as material is concerned, its format is excellent and it is well written. In my opinion a report of this type is an example to some other departments so far as the drafting is concerned. Anyone can read this report and get a general understanding of how the Post Office Department functions, and as far I am concerned I have no hesitation in giving all credit to the persons who compiled the report and to the printers. It is an excellent report. If by any chance the Postmaster General had a hand in this matter I will include him in my congratulations.

Without any doubt the efficiency of the department has been increasing over the years, resulting naturally from the expansion of the department, from experience and from changed circumstances, particularly the use of motor transport in highway service and things of that sort which make it possible for the department today to provide services that would not have been economic 10, 15, 20 or 30 years ago.
I think efficiency has been improved as a result of greater departmental diversification into more branches and the decentralization of the administration which I have noticed going on in recent years with respect to various facets of the department's operations and with respect to area or geographical administration. I think that the closer you can get the administration to the persons who are being administered the more satisfactory and efficient the administration is likely to be.
I wish to say a word or two about the engineering and development branch which has to do with buildings, equipment and things of that sort. I have read the report very carefully in that connection. When the minister replies to the various speeches that have been made will he assure the committee that there is no overlapping or duplication with the Department of Public Works? I should like him to define clearly for the benefit of hon. members the relationship between the engineering and development branch of the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works. I notice that the Minister of Public Works is listening very attentively and I am pleased.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Just for old friendship's sake.

I am interested in this matter because I know that, according to Parkinson's law, there is a tendency to build up branches and for duplication and overlapping to occur. I mention this matter because I have noted one or two things and have had one or two things brought to my attention.
We will say that a site is being chosen or alterations to a building are being considered by the engineering and development branch of the Post Office Department and naturally by the Department of Public Works at the same time. It has been drawn to my attention that an official of the engineering and development branch will visit an area and then later an official of the Department of Public Works will visit the same area. If there is any correlation between these departments I suggest it would be a good idea to have the two officials visit the sites or the buildings together.
Because it is the people's money that is being spent and because it is the local people who are directly concerned with the new

building or improvement, I also suggest that the local authorities should be consulted, whether it be the municipality or, if there is no organized community, a responsible body like the chamber of commerce or in certain cases a trade union or some other local organization. It is very irritating to local people to wait anxiously for years for the erection or the improvement of a building and then to read in the local paper that so and so from the Post Office Department visited the area in connection with the matter last week, or so and so from the Department of Public Works did so. Therefore I suggest that, if possible, these officials should visit these sites together and that there should be consultation with the local authorities or with the appropriate local organizations.
I have had it brought to my attention by quite responsible people, in fact on occasion even by supporters of the Conservative party who very often consult me in my riding, particularly about the Columbia, that these officials come and, as it were, steal away in the night unsung, unheard and unknown until the people read about their visit in the local paper. I should like the minister to explain the relationship between this branch and the Department of Public Works.
There is another branch mentioned in the report which was established in more recent years. I am not quite sure whether it was set up under the administration of the present minister although I think it was commenced before he became the lord almighty in this department. I refer to the public relations branch which is a very useful one. I have met members of the staff of this branch at various larger centres when they have been engaged in presenting an excellent exhibit and giving out information that created a better understanding of the administration of the department and how it functions. However, I have a suggestion to make in this regard, and I may say I am in a rather bright mood today. I had a good sleep last night.
I suggest that the officials would be well advised to visit the smaller places in my constituency. They have gone to places like Ross-land, Trail and Nelson-very important and nationally known centres-but many of the smaller communities have not had the benefit of this service. If it is possible, I suggest that these officials should visit the smaller centres where many people congregate for certain annual local events such as fairs and events put on by women's institutes. I am a great believer in getting the co-operation of the women's institutes in things of this sort because in my experience I have always found the ladies a great spur to understanding and action. In passing I might mention the important Inonoaklin valley fair held at
Supply-Post Office
Edgewood which draws people from a large area and which would be a very suitable centre for such activities. Then there are the Nakusp women's institute fair and the New Denver and Kaslo fairs. These fairs, in conjunction with those at Nelson and Rossland, are on a circuit. They all run consecutively during the month of September. I suggest it would be very easy indeed to have the officials who go to the Kootenays make the rounds of all these fairs. In that way they would inform a large number of people. At the same time the exhibit would be a nice contribution to a small fair. You will find that in the smaller places people pay a lot of attention to these things and are interested in them. So I make that suggestion to the minister in the very best spirit.
I have got to begin now to turn nasty, shall I say. I want to mention the question of patronage. Mind you, I give the government great credit in many respects for resisting the claims of those who would like to return to the days of patronage. I consider patronage an evil in a modern democratic society but I realize the difficulties. This matter has been brought to my attention even by some Conservatives and also by veterans and other citizens and I should like to mention one example. In fact, it is the only case in the minister's department that has been brought to my attention since I have been a member. I said I would raise this matter in the chamber. It is in connection with the appointment of a person to the post office in Trail.
I understand these appointments come under the civil service. You must remember that in Trail, as in other places, we have capable men and women, unfortunately including some members of the Progressive Conservative party, who are unemployed. The wife of the campaign manager of the defeated Conservative candidate was appointed to a position in the post office. Her husband is the principal of the high school, I am informed, and I understand he receives a good salary. I am not questioning the right of anyone to work, but under these circumstances it is most irritating to veterans, widows and young men and women who are seeking employment to find someone appointed to a position like this, particularly when the people are under the impression it was a political appointment. I should like the minister to inform the committee if there was a civil service examination in connection with this appointment. If there was, would he give us the names of the persons who wrote the examination and their marks, because there has been considerable criticism of this appointment. I said I would bring it to the attention of the minister.

In my opinion, patronage is something that should not be tolerated. I know all the weaknesses of human nature and it is very easy to drift into this situation. I give great credit to the former minister of public works for resisting all the pressure that was brought to bear on him in this connection. He is a man of great character and he stood against it. A party that stands against patronage benefits from that stand because you might please one person by a political appointment but you would create a great deal of dissatisfaction. I believe also that anyone who practises patronage under present day circumstances should be ashamed of himself.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to hear the shouts of "hear, hear" from the government benches opposite me.
Another matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister concerns the appointment of casual employees to the smaller offices. I understand that these people are paid by the department. I have had a number of associations, women's institutes and veterans' associations, bring this matter to my attention. I understand the veterans' preference is not being respected with regard to these appointments. I do not know whether or not this preference applies directly to these casual helpers, but these casual helpers usually end up on the permanent staff. I am speaking of post offices in which there is a postmaster and anywhere from two to five employees.
One instance which was brought to my attention concerned a person who was not a citizen and who was appointed as a casual employee. At the same time there were quite competent people, such as non-pensionable widows, who might have done the work. I do urge that consideration be given to this matter. When the minister replies, I should like him to inform me as to the basis on which casual employees are appointed to the smaller offices where, apparently, the postmaster is left on his own to make the selection and make recommendations. I should like to know whether or not, after these people are appointed, they come under the terms of the Civil Service Act or if any consideration is given to the veterans' preference.
I want to mention the buildings. I read something in a newspaper a day or two ago to the effect that Mr. Grosart had recommended that communities wanting post office buildings or public buildings should get in touch with their local Progressive Conservative Association. If he did that, he ought to be ashamed of himself, and I have no hesitation in saying so.
Where did you read that?

I have the newspaper up in my office, and I will ask another hon. member to deal with it later. In so far as public buildings are concerned, I usually listen to the representations of the chambers of commerce, the municipalities and other organizations. I can truthfully say that I make it a pracitce never to ask a minister to consider any such representations until I, personally, have visited the area and been convinced, in my own mind, that the building was essential. I have followed this practice throughout the years. I have been very fortunate in having this non-partisan spirit accepted in that respect. The chambers of commerce, women's institutes and municipalities have all respected men-not me personally because some of them think I am a bit odd-as the representative of the constituency. I believe that any lack of respect for a member's office disregards the principle of democracy and shows a lack of respect for the principles of democracy. I trust that Mr. Grosart's recommendation is not accepted by the communities or by the members of this house.
I want to say a word or two about stamps. I have quite a number of constituents who are very keen philatelists. In fact, any letters that come from foreign countries have to have their stamps removed carefully and I apportion them out every so often. As a matter of fact, my secretary and I have a sort of monthly circuit that we follow in apportioning these stamps. Not long ago the Trail Smoke Eaters won the world hockey championship and I asked the minister, at the request of the local people, if he would consider overprinting a northern development stamp or some other stamp as a means of celebrating this important victory.
This is the 60th anniversary of the founding of the city of Trail. It was most interesting that the Trail Smoke Eaters, a team composed mostly of smelter workers, should win the world's hockey championship for the second time. The minister said he had looked at the fire brigade stamp, and that was not appreciated by some of my constituents. Some of my philatelist friends in Trail have sent me this stamp issued by the government at Geneva celebrating this victory, yet the government of Canada does not even consider it worth while issuing such a stamp. Then, again, I have three stamps sent by other philatelists-I will send them over to the minister if he will promise to send them back because they must be returned-issued by the Soviet union to commemorate the winning of the world hockey championship by their team in 1957. I have told my constituents who belong to various philatelic societies, as well as the hockey fans, that I would raise the matter in the

house again and ask the minister if he did not think we could do as well as the Soviet union in recognizing the achievement of a great hockey team like the Trail Smoke Eaters.
I wish now to deal with one or two local issues. There has been in the city of Rossland a lot of interest with respect to the proposed new post office building or the alteration of the present one. The citizens generally are very favourably disposed toward the present site because it is central. Rossland is a city built on the side of a mountain, so one does not have much scope with respect to a site. The citizens are interested in maintaining the post office at the present site. I should like the minister to say what has happened to date in respect of the improvement of the present building and what the department is proposing. The village of Fruit-vale, a prosperous and growing community in a beautiful valley south of Trail, also has a great need for new post office facilities. The village council, rotary club, chamber of commerce, women's institute and all the other community organizations are very anxious to see a new post office building erected in Fruitvale to meet the needs of this expanding community. I should like the minister to inform the committee what is being done in this connection. He mentioned that the matter was being investigated and wrote me to that effect. I appreciate that, but for the information of my constituents I should like to know what is the state of affairs at the present time.
I must say the building of these small post offices was an excellent idea. The buildings are a credit to the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works, and they are appreciated. Small federal buildings in small communities intrude the personality of the government of Canada into these small communities. I think this program has been very worthwhile and I am glad to hear that other hon. members agree.
I have heard number of people mention that Canada is so vast that many local people are perhaps hardly conscious of the services and importance of the federal government of Canada. I think it was an excellent thing when the department decided to erect these small buildings in the smaller communities to a greater extent than ever before.
I want to mention one or two other matters. I have been asked to bring to the minister's attention the necessity for improving the ventilation in the Nelson and Trail post offices. Trail is the warmest part of our constituency because of our topography. Trail is located in the bottom of a valley and sometimes becomes very hot in the summer months. That 90205-6-233
Supply-Post Office
post office requires particular attention in this regard. I suggest that air conditioning be installed, or that there be an increase in the number of fans.
With respect to the Nelson post office- and I have been all through it and talked to the various people about it-there is still an unsatisfactory state of affairs with respect to ventilation owing to the lint that comes from the sacks which arrive there. I think it is the centre in which the sacks are opened, and then they are redistributed to other points and taken by mail carriers to various parts of the constituency. However, there is still some complaints about the amount of lint that is floating around in the air. I have no experience of this, although I have visited the post office, but I am told it is quite inconvenient at times and I bring this matter to the minister's attention.
We appreciate the rural mail services. I like the approach to these services and the changes suggested. I notice that the minister has had the local people sign a petition in order to express their wish for this or that service in respect to the arrival time of mail. I think this is an excellent suggestion. It gives the department an opportunity to accurately assess local opinion and determine whether these people would like the mail to come in at a certain time or later. I appreciate that being done, and so do the people.
At the Nakusp post office a petition was signed regarding whether the mail should come from Nelson at a certain time or later. Many people thought this was all right. Some were in favour of one time and some were in favour of another. The majority were very emphatic in one direction. But the point is. they were consulted. They felt they were consulted, and they were.
I think this is an excellent way to solve many of these problems that arise in local communities, where perhaps one or two people are listened to who are not always giving the department the accurate public opinion.
The residents in the Inonoaklin valley have asked for a daily mail service. The minister is looking into this matter. It is a growing community and I trust this question will receive favourable consideration.
I will cease at this point, Mr. Chairman, and look forward to the minister's reply. In the meantime I shall sit here and watch his beaming countenance with interest.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I do not give much credence to the statement made by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. The hon. member's statement was that the article about

Supply-Post Office
patronage appeared under the name of the national organizer of the Progressive Conservative party.
The hon. member asked that a stamp be printed to commemorate the Trail hockey team. I should like a stamp to be printed to commemorate the Lacombe Rockets who are at the moment sweeping their way across Canada in the intermediate championship series and I hope will be selected to represent Canada in the world hockey championship games next year.
My remarks on this item will be brief, but I could not let this opportunity pass without expressing, on behalf of the people of the Wetaskiwin constituency whom I have the honour to represent in this house, their very great pleasure and appreciation in the increased and improved post office services which they have enjoyed over the past three years.
These improvements have consisted of a great many things, but in a rural area, of course, the most important is rural delivery. New rural routes have been established, existing routes lengthened and the service increased from twice to three times weekly. There has been a general improvement throughout our rural services. As an hon. member said yesterday, mail is one of the most important services that people receive anywhere.
Improved post office facilities are being provided, and I would say to the minister that the people of the towns of Calmar and Devon appreciate being provided with the post offices which are now nearing completion. In addition, the proposed new building for which tenders have now been called in the town of Lacombe will be very much appreciated by the people of that town and the surrounding area.
When the new corner mail boxes are placed around the city the residents of the city of Wetaskiwin will express through me their appreciation of the minister and his department. I refer particularly to our senior citizens and the busy housewives, many of whom at present have to walk over a mile to post a letter.
Wetaskiwin is a growing city and is spreading out quite far. With one post office almost in the centre of the city it means a long and arduous walk for many of its inhabitants.
Unlike my hon. friends in the opposition I am not too concerned or fearful of the deficit in the operation of the minister's department, and I do not think the people whom I represent are fearful about it either. We realize that improved services cost money and we are willing to pay our share of those

costs in return for the vastly improved services which we have obtained over the past four years.
Mr. Chairman, I could not close my remarks without saying a word about the Post Office Department employees in my constituency. Perhaps, unlike my hon. friends and colleagues from urban and suburban areas, in my rural constituency I know every employee of the minister's department and count them among my friends. I wish to express to them my personal thanks and appreciation for their devoted and efficient service to their patrons.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words to congratulate and thank the minister, as well as the staff of the Post Office Department, for their devotion to the Canadian people.
I should like also to thank his office staff, including Mr. Guy Caron who politely replies to our letters or telephone calls, when we are in need of information.
I should like also to draw the attention of the house to the fact that a letter carrier service will soon be inaugurated in Repenti-gny and Charlemagne, a service which will be very helpful to the people of that part of my constituency.
For many years such a service was expected. Thanks to the co-operation of the Post Office Department, that service will become a reality and the people of my constituency will be on the same footing as that of Montreal.
I should like to emphasize the present situation at the Joliette post office. The staff there is cramped for space, on account of other services which are already set up there. The city of Joliette is growing, and the staff is cramped for space in the post office. In my opinion, the Department of Public works should consider the possibility of enlarging the post office and of increasing its staff.
The possibility of increasing the number of postmen to better serve the city of Joliette should also be considered. Thus, the hours of work could perhaps be reduced and better working conditions be provided for postal employees in Joliette.
I congratulate the government which, since it has been in power, has issued several commemorative stamps that illustrate very well our national history.
Such initiative emphasizes among our young people and the whole Canadian population the names of those who have worked for the greatness of our country.
That is quite a constrast with what used to be done formerly, when stamps were issued to illustrate, for instance, the Rocky mountain goat or some similar thing.
I hope that, in future the government will issue a commemorative stamp at least once a month to illustrate a phase of our national history. I understand that, for a good many

Supply-Post Office
years, the Post Office Department has had great difficulty in stopping the flow of foreign lottery tickets.
If, some day, the Criminal Code were amended to allow lotteries in this country, we would at the same time avoid the spread of foreign lottery tickets in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, those were the remarks I had to make, and once again I wish to congratulate the employees of the Post Office Department who are devoting themselves constantly in the interest of Canada.

Besides, at the time of the erection of the Joliette post office building, which has remained famous in political history, I believe that the Auditor General had strongly blamed the government for what was in fact an example of maladministration. I should like to again bring to the minister's attention the difficulties encountered by his department in the establishing of rural mail services. The minister referred to this problem in his opening remarks. I come from an area of Canada where two thirds of the population live in rural areas and I should like to again direct attention to the problem, of vital concern to the Postmaster General and the department, regarding revenue post offices. I am sure that every hon. member appreciates the criteria used in determining whether an area should be provided with a semi-stafled post office which, of course, is housed in a regular post office building under the management of a postmaster who is a member of the civil service.
Most of the postal services in the rural areas of Canada are carried out by revenue post offices, and very often the accommodation provided is grossly inadequate. This cannot be deemed to be the fault of the Postmaster General because, in the final analysis, the

individual conducting the business of a revenue post office must supply the accommodation, fuel and other overhead costs out of his income which is usually rather small because of the limited volume of service transacted.
The situation existing in rural Canada today has changed from that of 20 years ago because more Canadians have ready access to jet and regular air travel. As a result of this situation more Canadians are travelling to various parts of this country and the world, and in order to maintain contact with their business associates and families they are using the mail services to a greater extent. I think the time has now arrived, in this situation, for the Postmaster General to give consideration to the problem of devising some means of providing more adequate accommodation for carrying out the services of the revenue post offices.
I must confess that I do not possess the answer, but this is a very important function having to do with the transacting of government business in handling Her Majesty's mail. The service provided by these small post offices directly affects the lives and businesses of Canadians in all parts of the country. Perhaps some means could be devised wherein post offices could be provided-such as small inexpensive, prefabricated buildings-for these small rural areas in Canada which do not qualify for a semi-staffed post office. I feel something should be done so that the unfortunate situation that exists can be rectified. In my own constituency I have often witnessed long lines of people standing outside in all types of weather waiting for the sorting of mail, because the facilities provided are not adequate; perhaps just a farmer's kitchen. This problem is an acute one. I realize that one cannot expect to find beautiful post office buildings in every rural part of this country. However, I do feel something can be done to improve the handling of mail at this level. An improvement in the handling of mail in the revenue post offices would certainly expedite the service and give a tremendous uplift to the people living in areas served by this type of post office.
As an example of the situation which exists I can refer to my own constituency which is, for the most part, suburban to the city of St. John's where annually many thousands of dollars in postal revenue are, for very sound reasons, channelled by businessmen through the city post offices. They feel that the facilities provided by the revenue post offices in their villages are inadequate. One cannot expect a businessman to transact his postal

business-purchasing money orders and unemployment insurance stamps-in some individual's kitchen. I feel that the time has come for a reappraisal of this whole question of revenue post offices because the situation today is not at all the same as it was 10 years ago. I am sure that the Postmaster General in his genial and competent manner will give this problem serious thought, as he always does, and will find an answer at some early date.
