Mr. Chairman, at the risk of offending the modesty of the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton), and as this is my first opportunity, since my election in 1958, to speak on his departmental estimates, I am taking the liberty of congratulating him.
First of all, I have always been impressed by the human qualities of the minister and especially by the way he runs his department.
Mr. Chairman, like my colleagues, I do not wish to extend this debate unduly, but the fact remains that even though certain matters do not concern the country as a whole, they are nevertheless of importance to the people of an area or even of a riding, and it is with such matters that I should like to deal with for a few minutes.
In the matter of congratulations, I wish to thank the minister for the work done by his departmental officials, under his personal guidance, I am sure, or at least in a general way, with regard to the city of Beloeil and the vicinity. Beloeil is an interesting town on the Richelieu river in Vercheres riding, but forming part of the federal constituency of Chambly-Rouville.
Quite close to Beloeil, is the industrial municipality of McMasterville and opposite, on the other bank of the Richelieu river, St. Hilaire and Otterburn Park.
The over-all population of those four municipalities form a rather important urban area, and I must thank the minister for having given due consideration to the fact that those municipalities, even though they are independent legally speaking, depend on each other economically and socially, because they have common interests. That is what the department came to understand and that is why Beloeil, and other neighbouring municipalities, St. Hilaire, Otterburn and McMasterville, got a letter carrier service. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, far from taking jobs away, that has meant employment for several letter carriers and several clerks in the Beloeil post office.
Supply-Post Office
Back home also.

Of course, Mr. Chairman, there is a fly in the ointment. Whenever the department decides to organize a postal service and to classify it among the offices with a letter carrier service, certain postmasters or postmistresses may lose their job. True, the civil service commission gives them a chance to write exams and to qualify as postal clerks, but a person may, in certain cases, already be of a certain age and not be in a position to take outside work. Such is the case unfortunately of two persons in the Beloeil area, more specifically in St. Hilaire Station and Otterburn who have, for several years, devoted their energies to the postal service. I am telling this to the hon. members for Mai-sonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) and St. Denis (Mr. Denis) because those persons who had been employed under the Liberal administration found themselves temporarily unemployed, being unable to accept a clerical position in accordance with the terms of the Civil Service Act. But they were postmistresses and as such they deserve to have their case examined with complete sympathy. Since positions, attractive enough but insufficiently paid, were offered them, the Post Office Department should take charge of these cases because there are technicalities which cause friction between the Post Office Department and the civil service commission.
That is one of the drawbacks of this system for which personally I have no use, a system under which we have a commission which does not take into account the requirements of the department, for the reason that it is not within the department.
It is time we ask ourselves whether it would not be better to establish an effective personnel service within each department, in order to allow each department to operate on sound business principles. One may wonder if that would not be better than having a civil service commission too prone to disregard the needs of the particular department and which, for want of more flexible regulations, prevents postmasters with many years experience from qualifying for some other work.
I take the liberty of submitting these cases to the minister. I am however, fully aware that this situation existed under the former government as it does today.
Such things will happen, and they do not involve political considerations. But still those are things which bear on citizens' careers

Supply-Post Office
and jobs, and these particular cases deserve to be considered with sympathy by the department.
It may be a good idea when the time comes to revise the Civil Service Act to take into consideration these special cases.
I would also like to talk about the situation of the postmistresses and postmasters in suboffices. In my opinion, they are asked to remain at the service of the public about eight hours a day, and they are too often paid salaries not commensurate with the time they devote to the government's service. As a matter of fact, if, in assessing the postal service we take as a criterion service to the public instead of revenue, we must consider an increase in these postmasters' compensation.
Incidentally, it may be a good idea for the minister to disregard the criticism about the deficit; it is unjustified criticism anyway. If the Post Office Department is a department at the service of the public, its efficiency cannot be assessed only in terms of deficit or absence of deficit, even more when members of the opposition criticize on the one hand the increase in parcel post rates, and on the other hand, berate the minister because he wants to reduce costs. I wonder what they are after.
There is also the case of the rural mail carriers, or contractors who distribute the mail on what is called a rural route.
Mr. Chairman, since a letter carrier service was established in Beloeil, in my constituency, I have compared the work done by a letter carrier who works so many hours and receives rather a good compensation for our area, even though there is room for improvement in the work of such contractors. I have yet to hear criticism from the letter carriers about their compensation, because if we compare the work of a letter carrier to the work of a rural mail carrier who has to supply his own vehicle, who works almost as long hours as the letter carrier, who has to give bond, and who must, in a word, prove that he is responsible and has qualifications equal to those of the letter carrier, I do not see why the government would not revise the rate of compensation, particularly with regards to the calculation of yearly mileage, which in my opinion is an important factor, at least as far as the setting of rates commensurate with the service rendered by a rural mail carrier is concerned.
I think it would be interesting if the government were to make an investigation in this regard.
Obviously, most of those who have rural route contracts do not work full-time like the letter carriers, but there again we must re-

member that a person who undertakes a contract must be available for government service several consecutive hours six days a week, which completely disrupts the balance of his daily routine. Even worse, it often happens that a carrier cannot quote on a second rural route because mail distribution on both is carried out at the same time to ensure a better service to the public. That situation prevents the rural carrier from having two contracts and thus earn a reasonable salary.
As I told the minister a moment ago, I have been happy to see all that has been done in municipalities like Beloeil, St. Hilaire, Otterburn, McMasterville. But there again a shadow mars the picture. The service has been working well enough, but the municipalities concerned are developing at such a pace that we shall soon have to consider building a new post office, I mean erecting a new federal building, either at Beloeil or St. Hilaire, for those are the two main municipalities, and the most centrally situated of that postal district.
I would therefore ask the minister to see that the officials of his department hurry up matters and, more particularly, make representations to the Department of Public Works so that a decision be made with regard to the matter. And as the service is working out well in Beloeil and the surrounding district, it might be well for the department to consider the possibility of extending such a service to a municipality like St. Bruno, in the constituency of Chambly, where the situation is about identical to that in Beloeil. For postal purposes, St. Bruno might be joined to St. Basile, and perhaps to a section of Beloeil or St. Hubert. St. Hubert is divided into various communities called parks, one of which, Croydon, has already a letter carrier delivery service, operated as a subdivision of the letter carrier service in Ville Jacques-Cartier. It would therefore be a question of organizing new postal routes from Ville Jacques-Cartier into those other sectors of St. Hubert.
Finally we have also the towns of Chambly and Marieville, which are in a similar position.
As far as Marieville is concerned, I would like to thank the department, as well as the minister, for having taken action, after considering my own representations as well as those of the municipality and of the town council, and I also want to congratulate them for deciding to enlarge the Marieville post office. Of course, some minor difficulties have arisen, but I think that the department will be able to settle things, if the new municipal

council co-operates as well as the former one. Of course, some people in Marieville should realize, that if they want their post office enlarged, the municipality must be sensible and ready to transfer or sell to the department for a reasonable price the site which it owns near the present post office, thus enabling the department to build in the most economical way.
Mr. Chairman, I would make a suggestion to the Postmaster General. I am not sure that the matter comes under his department, but I think he might do something to carry out what I am now submitting to the house. Voters in the various ridings of the province of Quebec are convinced that their representative has only 125 or 150 miles to travel to the Ottawa session, and that he has enough leisure to come home and meet them on week ends. It is often difficult for constituents to meet their elected member and unfortunately several of them do not even know that members are sitting throughout the week, and they have not the slightest idea that we are sitting seven or eight months a year. It might be worth while for the government to consider giving the members in each constituency one or two rooms in federal buildings, in post offices for instance, so that a member may receive his constituents, especially when the federal building is rather centrally located. It might be something worth trying since it happens that in some federal buildings there is always a room which is not used every day or every hour of the day by the employees of the Post Office Department. The employees of the Post Office Department, who are regularly in touch with the public, could give information to constituents wishing to meet their member and tell them when he would be available.
I already see the hon. member for St. Denis in an office in a Montreal sub-station getting information about the Post Office Department. Perhaps this might give him the opportunity to see for himself how well the Post Office Department is administered since the change of 1957 which was wanted by the public in general, whatever the hon. member for St. Denis may think.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to come back to the topic of congratulations and tell the Postmaster General how convinced we are that there has been a change, even in the Post Office Department, since that famous election in 1957, when the voters gave the
Supply-Post Office
Liberal party to understand that it had not inherited the power in Ottawa from God the Father.
Mr. Chairman, for the past three years, I did not have the opportunity of taking part in the debate on the estimates of the Post Office Department because our friends opposite took all the time available in this house for criticizing.
Since I have a few minutes left before my time is exhausted I wish to make a few remarks of a general nature on the administration of the Post Office Department.
First of all, I had the opportunity, at the opening of the new postal service in Beloeil, to meet the authorities of the Post Office Department. I met people in charge of key jobs in the administration of this department for the Montreal region. Whatever the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) may think, those people could smile easily, were in a good mood and seemed quite satisfied with their lot and proud of their minister. I do not believe them to be hypocritical to the extent of telling me about their satisfaction and telling different to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and the hon. member for St. Denis.
I heard the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont criticize the fridigity of the Postmaster General's speech. According to the hon. member there was no humanitarian consideration in the minister's speech and he nearly added that it lacked poetry. But where he contradicts himself is when he takes the minister to task for having presented his report as if he were a chairman of a board of directors.
After all, this man is in charge of a great concern for which he is answerable to parliament in every detail. The opposition blames him for acting like the director of a great concern. I cannot understand it.
I have listened with attention to the first part of the speech made by the hon. member for St. Denis, yesterday, but I did not have the courage to listen to the second part, even after a good dinner; I just glanced through the expurgated and corrected version which appeared in this morning's Hansard.
At all events, I should like to touch upon one point of the speech made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, who spoke about scooters. I wonder why the hon. member is against one aspect of mechanization which the Post Office Department might now adopt, when he demands himself a certain mechanization. Does the hon. member realize that, after having criticized the Post Office Department-because he claims that

Supply-Post Office
the staff will decrease on account of mechanization-he is proposing new improvements which mean some re-organization that might involve the dismissal of some employees?
I also note the congratulations offered by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, and no doubt also by the hon. member for St. Denis, to postal employees after having criticized them for half an hour. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, why the morale of those employees should be so low, as the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont claims, if not because of the unjustified criticism which is voiced against them, in order to splash the minister.
Mr. Chairman, I hope that after all those compliments, the minister will take into consideration the few remarks I made on behalf of my electors. I make my apology to the other members of the house for having taken so much valuable time and for shortening the holidays of the hon. member for St. Denis, but it was in the interests of my electors, and I believe I have done my duty.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Kootenay West referred to the problem of patronage in relation to the Post Office Department. Personally I am quite concerned about this matter. Certainly the Conservative party should be concerned about it as well as governments generally if governments are going to function in a democratic manner. So far as my riding is concerned, the story has appeared in newspapers across the country that Mr. Grosart, the national organizer of the Conservative party, came to the town of Haileybury in the riding of Timiskaming shortly before the Conservative party convention and told people there, at least two of them being town councillors, that if they wanted a new post office they had better have a delegation, under the auspices of the defeated Conservative candidate, make representations. He said that this was the way to do it, and the best time to do it would be at the Conservative convention.
This statement appeared in the local newspapers and I have no reason to doubt the integrity of the sources of information. There are several people who are closely connected through marriage with the defeated candidate in that area. I am quite sure that the information was correct. It could not matter less to me, one way or the other. If the people of Haileybury need a new post office and a new post office is warranted, then I will fight to get it. I feel this would be true of the Conservative candidate who was defeated at the last election. I do not believe there is anyone who represents a riding in this country who is not interested in getting these things for his riding.

Can the Postmaster General tell me or tell the country that he will give the town of Haileybury or any other place a post office on the basis of patronage, as something in repayment of certain considerations? Will he say that a post office will be built on that basis? Is it not true that in the majority of cases where post office buildings are constructed, the department sends out people to assess the facilities that are available and the number of customers using those facilities? Is it not true also that the Post Office Department sends out inspectors to assess the cost of renting a building as compared with the cost of erecting a public building? Are those things not done on a business basis as we have been led to believe they are? If they are, then what type of service does Mr. Grosart pretend to supply to these communities by lining up the councillors who are interested in obtaining a new building for the area?
Certainly, one cannot blame these people for being interested in a new building. They are told by someone who appears to be quite close to the federal cabinet that this is the way you have to do these things. I should like to give the former Conservative candidate credit because he did tell the council he would need a resolution from the council recommending the erection of a new public building in the town to house the post office. He suggested also that before he carried their representations to the convention-I presume that is where he went because these events occurred only a couple of days before the convention-he would also want a letter from the chamber of commerce and from other interested agencies.
The article appearing in the Northern News, Kirkland Lake, March 14, states in part:
Mr. Rice recently unsuccessfully sought action from government on waterfront improvements at Haileybury. Mr. Cook-
That is the mayor of the town.
-said the government did nothing about the defeated P.C. candidate's request then.
Even in these small communities politics enters into these situations because here you have the mayor, a Liberal, arguing with two or three of the councillors who hold positions in the Conservative organization.
The council did not authorize Mr. Haskett, to forward a copy of the resolution to Mr. Peters, C.C.F. member of parliament for the riding.
This is a "beef" on my part, Mr. Chairman, because I am the only one concerned. I make this grievance in the light of the fact the people seem to have been advised to ask the defeated candidate to look after this matter. If the councils were operated in this manner,

then you would have all the defeated candidates for council sitting in the council chamber. If you do not believe that democracy works-

In the Toronto Telegram, the edition of March 14. Incidentally, it may be of interest to hon. members to know that at the time the editor of the Toronto Telegram phoned me and asked me to comment on this particular matter.
I am not the only one who is concerned about this incident. I find a letter appeared in the Northern News of March 17, 1961, and I should like to read a part of it. The letter is signed "Democrat" from Charlton, Ontario. I have not the faintest idea who he is, and I know nothing about it. This is what the letter says:
In an account of a recent meeting of the Hailey-bury town council published in your paper it was reported that Foster Rice was being approached to act as a go-between with the federal government in the matter of having a federal building put up in the town. There is nothing wrong about the town wanting such a building and there is a need for one, but why get Mr. Rice to act as intermediary when there is already a man at Ottawa who is being paid to look after the interests of the riding. I refer to Arnold Peters, M.P. for Timiskaming. I am sure that Mr. Peters, our elected member, is as capable of presenting the case for the town as is Mr. Rice, the defeated candidate. Furthermore, I believe Mr. Peters is as keenly conscious of the needs of the district as either of the defeated candidates. It is all very well for our politicians to prate of democracy at election time but when they deny its very principles once the election is over, it is enough to make at least some of us wonder if those who sit in the seats of the mighty know what democracy really does mean.
I underline the words, "At least some of us wonder if those who sit in the seats of the mighty know what democracy really does mean."
In the last election three men ran for office. Two of them definitely were not elected. Therefore it became obvious to even the most obtuse of the
Supply-Post Office
electorate that the one who got the most votes was the one whom the majority of the people chose as their representative.
With three or more candidates in the field, it can scarcely be said that the term "majority rule" is now applicable. Our present political set-up with the old parties fighting tooth and claw has created a situation of which the C.C.F. has been quick to take advantage. Both Liberals and Conservatives would be well advised to smarten up and stop scrapping, otherwise the New Party will slip in and pick up more of the marbles.
I do not believe the last part of the letter is relevant to this issue. I do feel, however, that the opinion expressed in the letter is shared by many people across the country.
I have never even been asked by the town council of Haileybury to give consideration to a new post office. If the town wanted a new post office, then the obvious method would be to approach the sitting member of parliament. If the town did not wish to approach the member of parliament, and this is quite all right, then I think they should appeal directly to the Postmaster General. They should make their representations to him. I will give a lot less credit to the minister than I do if I find the department does not send inspectors to the area to investigate the facilities available, consider the number of people using the facilities, and reach a decision on the basis of such an investigation.
If we have an opposition member in a riding it should make not one bit of difference, in my opinion, whether or not the sought for post office is built. The post office should be built because there is a need for it, and for no other reason. I have not asked for post offices to be built in any area where I consider the facilities to be sufficient to serve the needs of the community. It is not my opinion that we should build new post offices every two or three years in a given area. We should build post offices to meet the needs of the community and do a satisfactory job in the area. I think that is what the Canadian people want, and it is certainly my opinion.
I have heard nothing more about this matter from either the council or any other source, but I will give the minister the credit I am sure he deserves. I am quite sure that if representations were made to the Postmaster General he did exactly what I have outlined, that is, he sent an inspector to examine the situation. I am quite certain the Postmaster General will say that the decision to build a post office in that area hinges entirely on the need and the information he receives from his own officials.
I was very pleased yesterday to sit in a committee of this house and hear representations from a group of civil servants who called themselves the postal employees' association, which is an organization closely

Supply-Post Office
connected with this department. They appeared to me, unlike most other civil servants, to be very aggressive and to have taken a progressive attitude towards obtaining a contract with their employer, and negotiations in general. In fact, they sounded almost like a trade union.
It has been my contention for a long time that civil servants who want to receive the benefits to which I think they are entitled will have to act more like trade unions. They will have to do more of the work themselves and get out and fight for what they want. They must put forward their views in an aggressive manner and be willing to do something about them.
Because of the attitude of this group I asked a number of questions of people closely connected with it. I did this to find out why the post office employees are more aggressive than other civil servants. I was surprised at some of the things I learned. I am told that a civil service clerk, grade III-I am not referring to a postal clerk-has to take an annual examination if he is employed in any one of the 14 district post offices in Canada. Upon the result of this examination depends a salary increase or decrease of $150 a year. If these civil servants do not pass the examination they do not receive an increase. More than that, if they do not pass the examination they are subject to a decrease in salary of $150 a year.
Therefore, when a grade III clerk employed in any one of the 14 district post offices takes the examination, in effect the examination is worth $300 a year to him. He has a chance to increase or decrease his salary by $150 a year.
If these civil servants fail to pass two of these examinations in one year they suffer the salary decrease I mentioned. Why should a civil service employee in the post office be treated differently from a grade III clerk in any other department of the civil service.
In addition to that, I should like to know from the Postmaster General why they are treated differently from the civil service grade III clerks in the headquarters of the post office, where they do not have to take an examination. Is it less important for them to be capable, on paper at least, through examinations, in the postal headquarters as it is in the district offices of the post office?
I should like to know, and I think the committee would be interested in the answer to this question, how many postal employees have suffered salary decreases because of these examinations. Also, what saving has this been to the operations of the Post Office Department?
In northern Ontario we have always been pleased with the fact that we have the benefit

of what is called the railway postal service sorting arrangement. This means that a letter leaving Kirkland Lake, rather than going to North Bay and remaining in the sorting process in North Bay for one day and coming back the following day to Englehart, we will say-only 30 miles away-and having a trip taking several days, will be put on the train and in an hour or so will be in the next town and will be dropped off there.
This service is being conducted through a sorting process on the trains. These employees must take these sorting examinations and obtain a mark of 97 per cent or they do not receive an increase in salary.
These examinations are exceedingly difficult. They create a great deal of tension. There can be as much as $300 riding on the result of an answer given in one of these tests. I wonder whether this is any advantage and whether it increases the efficiency of the department. I wonder whether these examinations are worthwhile. If they are not, why must they be continued?
This system means that in most cases employees, particularly those connected with sorting, have to take examinations at least twice a year and continue taking them until they are 60 years of age. It seems to me this is unreasonable and is something more than we ask of any other civil service employee.
In connection with this matter I should like to know what is the Postmaster General's justification for demanding that many of the department's employees themselves purchase the sorting cards and sorting test cases. Why is it that the department does not, after making the initial purchase of test cards and test sorting cases, supply these civil servants with the means of keeping them up to date? Why does the department demand that the employee himself pay for new test cards that are continually being put into use?
I understand that a terrific turnover and change-over of services is now taking place. These employees must have this current information. For instance, if one is sending a letter to Highland Grove, for instance, they have to know that it goes to Lindsay first and then it goes through another little town before it gets to Highland Grove, or that it goes to Highland Grove before it gets to Lindsay, and the next time the trucking arrangement may be such that the letter is taken to some other place.
In each case these cards have to be brought up to date, and they have to be paid for by the employee. Not only does the employee have to take these examinations, but the machinery necessary for him to carry out his work has to be purchased by him. It is not simply a matter of skill; it is a matter of

learning and study. This study has to be carried out in his own time and with his own equipment. This is an added burden to these employees.
I do not believe this is justifiable. I believe that if we wish to keep up the standard of our postal employees the least we should do is to supply them with the equipment necessary for them to keep their card indexes up to date. I think this expense should be borne by the Post Office Department.
I am sure the minister will know what these costs would be. He will be abe to give us an over-all figure of how much this system would cost the department. If the department were to supply both the initial test cards, the test cases and the revisions which are necessary from time to time, I am sure the Postmaster General could tell us what costs would be involved.
In the staffed post offices employees get an increase automatically in the first year on the recommendation of the postmaster. The second increase of $150 is granted only if the employee is able to pass a departmental examination, and from the second year onward, the point at which the employee reaches his maximum salary with an increase of $100 a year, he must pass two examinations a year and continue to pass those examinations, in order to remain at maximum salary, for 20 years. After 20 years employees still have to continue to take one of these examinations a year until they reach age 60.
It seems to me that this is requiring a great deal more from civil servants employed in the post office than is required from civil servants employed in any other department of government. I find this system hard to understand in view of the government's claim that it wishes to see equality of treatment as among all civil servants. In this case one employee is treated differently from another even in the same classification. It seems to me that if industry asked its employees to reach and remain at a high standard of knowledge it would at least give them time to do so during their working hours, provide instructions to enable them to keep up to date and, in addition, I am sure, the materials which would be necessary.
In relation to railway post offices I should like to know how many of these offices have been taken out of operation since the period when the number of these offices was at a maximum. I notice from the minister's report that in 1957-58 there were 208 and in 1958-59 only 96. I should be interested to know what the number was in 1959-60 and the estimate for the year 1960-61.
I should also like to ask the minister what is the intention of the department in relation to highway post offices. These are vehicles
Supply-Post Office
equipped with racks and sorting tables together with other facilities needed for the sorting of mail, and a great deal of use is already made of them in the United States. In many respects they resemble closely the railroad cars designed for the sorting of mail in transit except that they have been converted for travel on the highways. We should be putting the railway sorting cars on tires, as it were, and allowing them to continue the service in those areas where transportation of mail by rail has been discontinued. I should like to draw attention to one example which is brought to my attention regularly and that is the area of Cochrane North where the service is curtailed generally. In order to reach this area from Toronto by rail one has to make two or three changes and delays take place even in the best of times, delays which affect, of course, the transport of mail as well.
Now that there is no sorting done along the route letters which are collected in the course of the journey have to be sent, sometimes, 200 miles from the source and then, in certain cases, must be returned 175 or 180 miles to the nearest village and considerable loss of time is incurred. I expect the minister has given consideration to the subject and that it will not be long before we see post office bus services travelling along the highways and before the same type of service which has been given to communities in the United States will be extended to us is Canada.
The advantages enjoyed as a result of sorting en route were, of course, considerable. They were advantages of some importance. For example, I might point out that communities along the line of the Ontario Northland Railway get at least a daily service of mail from Toronto. Yet I have been in places such as Collingwood, Dundalk in Grey-Bruce where letters have taken as long as five days to arrive. It would have been quicker to have gone to Toronto to pick them up. One of the endeavours of the Postmaster General should be, by the use of this new type of sorting vehicle, to provide a service equal to that enjoyed by townships along favourable rail routes.
I should like to mention one other matter, and it is one which affects politicians as much as it affects anybody though I believe it will concern all those who are interested in mailing through the use of a directory. I should like the minister to give a fairly extensive explanation of the means used to bring these postal directories up to date, because I am convinced that the one I use has never been revised. In that rural mail directory there are the names of people who have been dead for four or five years. In addition, there appear names of people who to my knowledge have left the country three or four

Supply-Post Office
years ago leaving their farms vacant. Every time I get a new copy of the directory I expect that at least the names of those people will have been removed but they still keep turning up. If you send letters to constituents using a rural mail delivery list you get back 25 per cent of those letters in many cases.
The situation is even worse in the urban areas where more than 25 per cent of the letters I have sent have been returned. It may be that some of the communities concerned are undertaking new zoning arrangements-arrangements which have not, to date, been completed-and this may bring in some element of confusion. However, it seems to me that in some cases as much as one third of the mail is returned stamped "address unknown". I believe the postal authorities make an effort wherever possible to deliver these letters. I am not completely in agreement-neither do I disagree-with those who say that mail from the House of Commons is considered to be second or third class material. Nevertheless I believe the volume of mail we get back is an indication of how badly the record in these directories is kept.
I am sure the minister realizes that something must be done in order to ensure publication of a much more up-to-date directory. Arrangements should be made to ensure that we get information as to changes in the areas back to the Queen's printer so that the rural directories are never more than six or eight months out of date when they are published. Some of them are a great deal more out of date than that. In many of the rural communities such inaccuracies are not excusable because the mail carriers and the postmasters or postmistresses know everybody in the area and are in a position to bring the directory up to date in a few minutes.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to unduly delay the passing of the minister's estimates, but I should like to make a few brief comments and shall do so as quickly as possible.
I should like first of all to refer to Post Office Department property. I am from an area which has not always had the privilege of having federal government services. Because I am from an area of that type I would imagine I am a little more jealous of these services than are those hon. members of the House of Commons who have always been accustomed to having them. I feel that, in a town or city, property that is normally called the Canada post office should be as well maintained as is any other institution in that city or town. In the area from which I come there exist a small number of large post offices which are kept as well inside as

any post office I have seen on the mainland, but considering the outside appearance of these buildings this is not so.
I recognize, as I am sure the Postmaster General will tell me, that the responsibility for maintaining these buildings lies with the Department of Public Works. However, responsibility is one consideration and interest another. I should suggest to the hon. gentleman that while he may not have the responsibility for maintaining the physical appearance of these buildings and properties I am sure he has a real interest in this regard.
On a recent occasion I went into one of our public buildings and asked an employee there why the building was well maintained inside while the grounds outside were so poorly kept. He replied that it cost a good deal of money to maintain the grounds in a manner comparable to the grounds around other buildings in the city. While that statement is perhaps true, and whether the responsibility is that of the Department of Public Works or the Post Office Department, something should be done in this regard. As a member of the House of Commons I would like to see all federal property maintained inside and out as well as possible.
I would suggest to the minister that he instruct those officials, who visit these institutions commonly known as Canada post offices, to see that these buildings are maintained in a proper fashion. I would suggest that the grounds outside should be kept in a manner compatible with other buildings belonging to the federal government. I would suggest that those areas around these post offices which are considered to be lawns, be kept as lawns so that individuals passing the property, whether they be Canadians or visitors to this country, will realize that the property is being maintained as well as one would expect it to be. Many individuals judge performance by physical appearance, and I refer not only to Canadians but also to those who visit our country during the warmer months of the year. I offer these suggestions very sincerely to the Postmaster General.
I have a few general comments to make and then will specifically refer to the northern part of my riding.
Before Newfoundland became a part of Canada in 1949 it did not have post offices as we know them today. At that time the post office services and telegraph services were combined under one department and the individuals operating these services for us were not only paid as postmasters but also as employees of the telegraph company. This situation exists to some extent today and presents a very real problem.
The individuals to whom I refer perform a service for the Post Office Department and

receive a salary in that regard. At the same time they work for the Canadian National Telegraph Company and receive a salary commensurate with the functions they carry out in that regard. I must say that some of the salaries paid are exceedingly small. I have written the Post Office Department officials in this regard and have been informed that the individuals to whom I referred were being paid on the basis of the amount of work they carried out. I then wrote a similar letter to the Canadian National Telegraph Company and was informed that the same individuals were being paid salaries by this company on the basis of the services they performed for it. This problem is batted back and forth between the Post Office Department and the telegraph company.
The minister might well suggest that instead of speaking in generalities I should present a specific case. I will mention an actual case which the minister will be able to understand. There is an assistant postmaster at Flower's Cove, Newfoundland, by the name of Calvin Whalen. He acts as the assistant postmaster as well as the messenger for the Canadian National Telegraph Company. The post office in which he is employed is responsible for distributing mail for 11 settlements and four other post offices serving a population of 2,000. This man receives, as a postal employee, a salary of $48.50 per month.
I do not know where the responsibility for this situation lies, but when I listened to the Postmaster General refer to increases in salary yesterday, I felt that I should bring this situation to his attention. I know that he will give generous attention, as he always does, to the problem I present. He is always very generous in his attention to problems I bring forward and, in saying that, I do not mean he always gives me the things I would like to have. While he does not accede to all my requests he always furnishes the reason why he cannot. In this day and age it is certainly disgraceful on the part of this federal government department to pay a salary of $48.50 per month to an individual whether or not he is working part-time for the Post Office Department and part-time for the Canadian National Telegraph Company.
My hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo as well as the hon. member for St. John's East, for whom I have a good deal of respect, mentioned a peculiar situation which exists in Newfoundland, and I refer to revenue post offices in small settlements. I realize that because of the amount of service provided by these offices as compared with that provided by the post offices in cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa and Halifax, higher
Supply-Post Office
salaries than those being paid today are not warranted. However, I suggest to my hon. friend that there is just a little more to it than this.
Let us take a small community where mail is delivered twice a week. This means that while mail is delivered only twice a week, the postmaster or the postmistress has to be on duty for the whole week. I could give instances where the amount of money paid for the month's service by the post office would not be sufficient to pay a charwoman to clean up after the mail has been delivered, and yet today the postmaster has to provide premises and services and the heat and light required to operate the post office in that small community.
In the larger towns and cities, of course, the criticism I am making does not apply at all. I agree with hon. members who have spoken before me that it is about time the Post Office Department paid some special attention to the problems of the revenue post offices. As I said before, we must have a good deal of respect for the service which we are able to offer to the public. We can have respect for those services and demand respect from others only if the services we provide are respected by the very people who initiate them.
I would hope the time is not too far distant when those who operate the small revenue post offices, whether they be in Newfoundland, Ontario or British Columbia, will receive in remuneration a salary not in terms of the volume of mail handled but in terms of the responsibility which they hold in the community in which they live. In my own home city the employees of the postal department are people who have that dedication to duty about which the minister spoke yesterday. I do not think he is wrong when he says that the employees of the Post Office Department are people who are dedicated to their jobs. I think he is right when he says this. On many occasions I have reason to go and visit those people and to ask things of them. They have always been very courteous and very willing to do those things which come within their responsibility. I think those individuals are a credit to the federal service and I wish to pay tribute to those individuals in my area who are employees of the Post Office Department. I know that in many instances they have trials and tribulations which are not usual in the larger centres. They have accepted those with good grace and have given service beyond that which the department would expect of them.
A few months ago I had occasion to ask the Postmaster General what provision was being made for the landing of mail from

Supply-Post Office
the C.N.R. boats in a settlement on the north coast of Newfoundland by the name of Bartlett's Harbour. The Post Office Department has made provision for the mail to come from the post office to the jetty wharf. The mail has to be taken from the jetty wharf to the boat which, because of the local land conditions, is some distance from where the C.N.R. boat is able to anchor, about one and a half miles. I was disturbed by the fact that the man who was paid to carry the mail from the post office to the jetty warf also, in order to get the mail on the boat, had to put it on board a small motor boat and carry it another one and a half miles to get it on board the C.N.R. boat.
When I asked the minister what arrangement was made for this mail to be taken from the jetty wharf to the boat and back he said that arrangements had been made with the C.N.R., or with the authorities, which would be the C.N.R. I am asking the hon. gentleman whether he will check on that again. A few months ago when I had occasion to check on this I found out that the arrangements which the Postmaster General thought were in effect were not being carried out. I would hope that in this particular instance the Postmaster General or his officials would make sure that if arrangements have been made by the department to have this mail delivered, and if the expenses of having the mail delivered are being paid by the department, the department is receiving the service for which payment is being made.
I now come to a point that is rather a sore one with me. Yesterday, my hon. friend suggested that there was no patronage in his department. It would be a little difficult -maybe I should put it more strongly-to convince me that this is true. I do not blame the Postmaster General for this, but in the area from which I come the Postmaster General or his officials will have a lot of trouble convincing me, or the people whom I represent, that patronage is not being practised in the Post Office Department. Again I say that I am not blaming the Postmaster General for it.
I will give one instance. If the hon. gentleman would like in private the name of the place and of the person, I shall be glad to give the information to him. We have an instance of a post office inspector coming to a certain place in Newfoundland looking for somebody to take over the post office. Because they need a post office in this place one fellow says, "I will take it". He takes the post office as a revenue post office. He remodels the lower flat of his home so that space will be provided for the post office and he carries on the normal operation of

the post office in that area. All at once something happens. One night after dark the post office inspector walks in and says to the postmaster, "We are taking the post office away from you". Everything belonging to the post office is taken from one place and moved to another after dark.
Here is a man who has spent a lot of money to remodel the lower flat of his house to accommodate the Post Office Department. The cost was far greater than anything he received from the Post Office Department. I cannot agree that this is the type of thing which a federal department should be doing. If this man is to be relieved of his duties, then I think he should be told in a proper way. I asked the Postmaster General a question in the house and he replied to me that the man was relieved of his duties because his appointment was only temporary. Surely, if the man's appointment was only temporary, he should have been told of this and then he would not have gone to the expense of changing over the lower floor of his house to accommodate the Post Office Department. What the reason for this is I am not going to say, Mr. Chairman; I am going to leave that to the imagination of the Postmaster General. But I do not believe this type of operation is in keeping with the dignity that we ought to attach to any federal department.
I now come to a regional area of my province, and one with which I am particularly concerned. I refer to the northern part of Newfoundland. The northern part of Newfoundland is commonly known as the Straits of Belle Isle, an area which is in one sense rather densely populated in terms of Newfoundland settlements. From Anchor Point in the south straight through the Straits of Belle Isle to Eddys Cove east we have a population of about 2,500 people. Some time ago I wrote the Postmaster General requesting that some provision be made for the building of a post office in this area and after due investigation he replied that he thought the existing space was sufficient for any duties the Post Office Department had to carry out. I am going to read a few words from his letter. He said:
As the space available is sufficient for our needs at Flower's Cove-
However, in the preceding paragraph he said:
The possibility of erecting a mail shed to further solve this problem is also being considered.
If the space in the existing post office is sufficient to take care of the business of the Post Office Department at the present time, then there is no need to build a shed. I do not know where the Postmaster General got his

information. I have been there and I know the situation. I know he has not been there although he has visited a number of places in my riding. I appreciate his visits and I extend an invitation to him to come again. If the Postmaster General were able to visit this area, as I have on a number of occasions, I think he would agree with me that the accommodation provided at Flower's Cove to serve 11 settlements both winter and summer is not sufficient to look after the mail operations in that area.
Although I have had a letter from the Postmaster General dated November 10, 1960, stating that the facilities provided at Flower's Cove are sufficient to look after post office operations there, I suggest to him that a second look needs to be taken at the matter. I say again to him that if he were to visit this area as I have on a number of occasions he too would realize that the facilities provided at Flower's Cove are not at all in keeping with the amount of work that has to be done.
Flower's Cove is situated nearly at the northern tip of Newfoundland. It has always been the commercial centre of the area and it is now becoming the educational centre. It has always been the religious centre of the area and has always been the centre of post office operations. With the increase in population, mail service and the amount of mail that individuals receive, this post office is no longer able to look after the requirements of the people. In view of all this I suggest to the Postmaster General that he take a second look at this northern part of Newfoundland to see if he cannot do something to improve the postal service in that area so that when he comes back to parliament next year and reports on the work of the Post Office Department he will be able to say to his credit that he has done something for one of the outlying areas of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, in commencing my remarks I should like to make a very short reference to the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Timis-kaming. The hon. member referred to a recent petition concerning a request for a new post office in his riding. All members of parliament and ministers receive a great many petitions on many subjects. The hon. member did not tell us how the petition came to Ottawa. I presume it could have come through the mail or have been delivered personally to the Postmaster General if Mr. Rice attended the Conservative convention. Regardless of who delivered the petition, I suggest that this incident proves only one thing to me, that the minister's door is open to all
Supply-Post Office
citizens; members of parliament, defeated candidates and the public at large.
Many congratulations have been extended to the minister, the senior officials and all other employees of the department. I have a few brief remarks to make and I do not want them to be taken as criticisms but rather as suggestions. First of all, I have received a great deal of correspondence containing criticism with respect to the loss of identity by small communities. This happens when a new rural route is established. Rural routes are generally desired by the patrons and I know they are accepted as an improved type of service. However, in almost every case when a post office is closed and a new rural route service is inaugurated communities of many years' standing lose their identity on the map. I do not know what the solution is because I understand that a rural route must start from a post office. However, it seems to me that in some cases more consideration could be given to the designating of rural routes and perhaps some formula could be worked out whereby communities that have been in existence for a number of years, communities having small boards of trade and business establishments, could continue to keep their original postal names and thus maintain their identity in the country.
Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Middlesex West made a plea for letter carrier service for the smaller towns. At the present time many suburban areas adjoining cities and larger towns where letter carrier service is in existence automatically qualify for home-to-home letter carrier service. On the other hand, in many rural areas small post offices are closed and the people receive the advantage of rural route service which is quite comparable to letter carrier service because there is door-to-door delivery.
However, there are many smaller towns across the country, particularly in the mari-times, with a population under 5,000 or between 5,000 and 8,000, which will never qualify for letter carrier service for generations to come. This is a situation that is causing a great deal of criticism of the Post Office Department. Resentment-I think that is the best word to use-is aroused by the fact that in suburban areas there is automatic letter carrier delivery service-if the adjacent city had such service-and by the replacement of revenue post offices in the country with rural routes and thus door-to-door delivery while residents in towns of 5,000 people must still rely on a semi-staff post office and the type of service they have had for years and years.
While dealing with letter carrier service there is one other point I should like to bring to the minister's attention for his considered opinion. I refer to the extension of letter

Supply-Post Office
carrier service. In the last two or three years there have been two or three extensions of letter carrier service in the city of Moncton, New Brunswick. In some cases it took months and months after the service was approved before it was finally started and in other cases the service went into effect very soon after it was authorized.
The reason for the delay in some areas is the requirement that 80 per cent of the patrons must have letter slots, street numbers, walkways, et cetera. I know that the service cannot become effective and efficient until there is 100 per cent co-operation with respect to these requirements. However, in some cases a few citizens refuse to co-operate and consequently the majority of the patrons who wish the service must wait indefinitely for the 80 per cent requirement to be met. I suggest to the minister that the standard might be reduced to about 65 per cent, and then after a short waiting period the service would eventually be put into operation and become 100 per cent effective.
I see my time is almost exhausted, Mr. Chairman, because of the hour, but there are two points I should like to mention. I should like the minister to take a look into the delivery of mail from the main post office at Moncton to the C.N.R. terminal. At the present time there is a large C.N.R. redevelopment taking place and I suggest this is an ideal opportunity for the construction of a tunnel for the transportation of mail from the post office to the terminal building. The procedure suggested would eliminate very serious traffic congestion on main street immediately adjacent to the post office building.
I should also like to thank the minister for the construction of two new post office buildings during the past year, and urge that more and more semi-staff offices be housed in federal buildings. This is something that small communities want, and it is something to which our citizens are entitled. If you go through the country you will find oil companies erecting new service stations, and banks new buildings, and in some cases- not too many in my riding-very poor accommodations rented and occupied as semi-staff offices.
I want ot thank the minister for his attention. Notwithstanding the criticism that he has received from some quarters, he can be assured that the majority of the members, the patrons of the post office and citizens of the country appreciate the fact that last year we received excellent postal service. We know that, as a result of the debate yesterday and today, this service will be improved next year.

I have a few remarks to make on this item. I should like, first, to commend

the Postmaster General upon the fine service he has given to the people of Canada generally. The people of St. Boniface are quite satisfied, as are the people in the town of Transcona, which is soon to be a city, and has personal delivery service instituted as well as drop mailing rate. Many sub-post offices are to be opened in the Windsor park area of St. Boniface. Two new sub-post offices were opened this year, one at Landmark and the other at Navin. I understand that plans are being made for a large post office in St. Boniface, and probably we will receive the details of that from the Minister of Public Works.
I should like to say a word about the very small post offices, many of which do not earn more than $300 or $400, out of which the operator has to pay rent. Unless the people operating such post offices have some other source of income it is very difficult for them to continue to operate these post offices. I know that at Charleswood it was impossible to get anyone to take the post office because they were required to keep the building open, and it was neither a home nor a business place.
Last year I suggested to the minister that we issue a stamp commemorating the religious aspect of Christmas rather than its commercial aspect. I was very pleased to learn that two other hon. members have joined in making this suggestion to the minister. Since Canada is a country that is about 99 per cent Christian, I do not believe there would be any objection if the Nativity scene were depicted on the 2-cent stamp. I believe this suggestion would be well received.
The last speaker touched upon a matter upon which I should like to touch, that is, the loss of identity of some post offices. In the case of St. Boniface, it is not quite loss of identity but last year the department gave people the option of addressing their mail to St. Boniface 6 or Winnipeg 6. The city of St. Boniface passed a resolution opposing this move. I believe the premier of Manitoba has written the minister in respect of this matter and I hope the minister will do what he can to restore unimpaired the name of the old city of St. Boniface. This would be greatly appreciated because St. Boniface is the oldest city in western Canada and, in addition, the name should be retained because of its historical connotation.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house is very simple and straightforward. I hope it will command not only some vocal support in the house but some positive support at this stage of second reading, when I hope a vote will be taken.
I think a bill such as this is an important measure. I think it is very important to the Canadian people that when a person goes to a lending institution to obtain a loan, or obtains money on an instalment credit plan or otherwise, the principle should be followed of setting forth in clear and specific terms the interest charges to be made.

This bill would require that in advertising there be a clear indication of the interest rate that will be charged to any prospective borrower with regard to any loan. The explanatory note of the bill reads:
The purpose of this act is to amend the Small Loans Act, so as to require any moneylender or small loans company, in any advertising in which the amount required by way of monthly or periodic payments in order to repay a loan is indicated, to state what the cost of such loan amounts to in terms of percentum per annum.
This would mean the prospective borrower would know the actual or the simple interest that would be charged on the loan.
I have placed companion legislation on the order paper. It has been debated on previous occasions. This companion legislation would have reduced the interest rate on small loans to 1 per cent per month or approximately 12 per cent per year. It was aimed at clipping the wings of loan sharks and providing a fixed limit of interest on money put out by money lenders.
However, the Conservative party are hand in hand with the loan sharks and these money-lenders and they are quite happy that these people should keep on pilfering the public. They are quite happy that these pirates in the money lending field should be allowed to go on filching the ordinary person who has to borrow money by charging extortionate rates and reaping profits that are scandalous in a modern society.

I think a more effective way of dealing with this problem is to educate individuals seeking loans to the idea of inquiring what interest rate and cost is being charged. Unfortunately, individuals making these loans neglect to read the contracts they sign, and do not insist that interest rates be set out.
I am familiar with an incident which will perhaps illustrate what happens to individuals making purchases on an instalment plan. A young couple buying a car had fortunately made arrangements to obtain a loan from a bank at the regular interest rate. Prior to their closing the deal with the car salesman they mentioned this fact, but were informed that it was not necessary for them to take advantage of the arrangements they had made because the company from which they were buying this car could finance it at 6 per cent interest. This young couple did not read the contract carefully-sometimes I suspect that contracts of this type are not even filled in at the time of signing-and did not realize

In this case I feel that the young couple, as well as the salesman, were at fault for the difficulties in which they found themselves. They were at fault, I suggest, in not reading the contract thoroughly before signing it. I would like to strongly warn individuals who are signing contracts of this kind to read them thoroughly and not be hurried into signing blank contracts, as I suspect many individuals are doing today. Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill No. C-19, an act to amend the Small Loans Act, advertising, I should like to say at the outset that I am much in favour of what is spelled out in the bill. As I understand the purpose of the bill, it is to amend the Small Loans

As the situation is now, small loans companies or other lenders are not required to state a certain rate of interest that they intend to charge for loans or the terms of the agreement as far as repayments are concerned. I think it is very important that it should be stated in any advertising or in any agreement what the interest rate is going to be and what the terms of the agreement are.
I must say that I view with some apprehension the action of some small loans companies and also some moneylenders when they do not set forth in their advertising the interest rate and also their repayment plan. This, of course, does not apply to all small loans companies and money lenders. I want to make that perfectly clear. I do not want to leave the impression that all small loans companies and moneylenders are taking advantage of their clients because they have not advertised their interest rates and the terms of their repayment plans.
Small loans companies are performing a very commendable service in this country but for the protection of the public from unscrupulous lending agencies the government should take action to protect the public either through the proposed amendment to the Small Loans Act or in any other legislation which will achieve the same result, namely, to have the small loans companies and other lending institutions advertise their interest rates and also their repayment plans.
In the case of many small borrowers it may be the first time they have availed themselves of loans and some of these people may not be familiar with the set-up of these lending agencies. However, if the interest rates and repayment plans are advertised they may seek advice from friends or other persons familiar with this kind of business and obtain information before going to a lending institution and committing themselves to something they will regret later. From past experience in serving on a credit union board in my home town I know that an individual wanting to obtain a loan needs all the information he can get beforehand. He should know what he is faced with as far as the interest rate is concerned, the repayment plan and any other agreement to which he commits himself when he signs the contract for the loan.
Since advertising and interest rates come under the jurisdiction of the government 1

think it would be in the best interests of those people who wish to obtain loans to make it obligatory for lending institutions to state their interest rates and also their repayment plans in their advertising. I can really see no disadvantage to small loans companies and other moneylenders in their being asked to state their interest rates in their advertising. There is nothing else I should like to see done at the present time and I have nothing to add except to say that the house should give serious consideration and approval to the bill and the proposed amendments as spelled out therein.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill No. C-19 which has been introduced today is to amend the Small Loans Act in order to require any moneylender or small loans company coming under federal jurisdiction to state in any advertising in which the amount required by way of monthly or periodic payment is indicated in order to repay the loan, what the cost of such loan amounts to in terms of per cent per annum. I may say that the principle of the bill is one that I accept wholeheartedly. I think there is wide agreement among hon. members of the house that some legislation of this type is needed.
Many hon. members feel that this is not exactly the type of legislation that is required, but I am sure that they and, indeed, those of the other place would like to see this problem examined very closely and legislation of some type brought in to effect the principle set forth in the bill. I think all hon. members will agree that today more than ever before there is a need for some control of advertising in the consumer lending field.
Over the last decade or so there has been a great growth in consumer credit. We have seen the sources of financing of many of the things we buy today change in this period. There was a time when the money required to finance the purchase of household articles, automobiles and all manner of personal chattels was obtained through the banking system. Today many retailers set up the financing required for articles of this kind or the purchaser will be referred to the finance companies, the acceptance corporations or the credit union. These are the leading types of consumer credit organizations in the modern world.
Since I have mentioned the credit union, I should like to take a moment to express to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house my own experience in the credit union work. As all hon. members know, credit is often more difficult to obtain in rural areas than it is in urban areas of Canada. The credit union has helped a great deal in this field. In my own

riding, the obtaining of credit is perhaps the largest difficulty that faces the farmer or fisherman who tries to become established as an economic business unit. In many cases, the credit that he could not otherwise have obtained has been available to him through the credit union, through the co-operation of his friends and neighbours who have joined with him in this very worth-while financing operation.
It is important also to note that perhaps the most important work credit unions have done has been in the educational field. Many people, not only in rural areas but in our urban centres as well, formerly knew very little about even rudimentary financial operations, but as a result of the operations of the credit unions they have learned a lot about what money can do, what it costs and from where it comes. It has been my good fortune for over a dozen years to be a member of a credit union and for perhaps a third of that time to have served on the credit committee of that organization. During those years I was forcibly impressed with the assistance given by credit unions to people who otherwise found the ordinary channels of credit closed to them. I can certainly say to the members of the house that any support they are able to give to the credit union movement or to the work these organizations are doing, will prove of great service to the people of Canada generally.
I have often wondered whether or not there was any way in which this parliament could give encouragement to the credit union by making funds available. The source from which the capital of the credit union is drawn is not the wealthiest segment of the population. These organizations provide credit, not only for education but for other purposes, to people who would otherwise have very narrow sources of credit.
In so far as Bill No. C-19 is concerned, my first impression upon reading it was, why should any moneylender object to setting forth the interest rate which he is charging his customers? Certainly, in so far as any other type of lending is concerned, through the banks, mortgage companies or under the National Housing Act, the interest rate is made known to the borrower. There is no attempt made to hide it from him. There is an area of financing in which interest rates are hidden, as some hon. members have said here today. I think we all know that this is true. I see no reason why we should not ask corporations which lend money in
Business of the House
the consumer field to show, in their advertising, what rate of interest they are charging. I think nothing could be fairer than that we ask the lender to tell the borrower how much he is being charged for the use of the lender's money. I wonder, however, if it might not be more prudent to have the bill referred to one of the standing committees of the house, perhaps the banking and commerce committee, for a thorough examination of the problem.
The day will come, I am sure, when we will have to invite the provincial governments to join with the federal government in enacting legislation which will cover all aspects of financing in Canada, not only consumer financing but the mortgage field as well. In view of the high interest rates charged on second mortgages throughout the country, I am sure many borrowers woud be better off if some joint effort were made by the provincial and federal governments towards the establishing of comprehensive, overall legislation to regulate financing in Canada. Certainly no such legislation could cover all aspects of the situation unless it were the result of a joint effort of the provinces and this parliament because many of the aspects of finance come under provincial jurisdiction while only a small part comes under the jurisdiction of this parliament.
I conclude by saying that, along with other hon. members who have spoken, I support the general principle of this bill. I should like to see the matter examined further by a committee of this house. I should be very surprised if many voices were raised in opposition to the general principle that the rates being charged by financing concerns should be shown in their advertising literature.
